sources.name: Hamel Husain & Shreya Shankar — Why AI evals are the hottest new skill

note: Companion to llm-evaluation-frameworks.json — that deck covers the tool vocabulary (RAGAS/DeepEval/Promptfoo), this one covers the underlying process a good eval workflow follows.

cards.front: What is “open coding” in LLM error analysis?
cards.back: An informal note describing the first specific thing wrong in a trace — written before you try to categorize it.

cards.front: What comes after open coding in the workflow?
cards.back: Using an LLM to synthesize the open codes into axial codes — named failure-mode categories.

cards.front: Why must an LLM-as-judge evaluator be binary (pass/fail), never a 1–5 scale?
cards.back: Likert-style scores on LLM judges are unreliable and hard to act on. Binary keeps the signal clean and forces an actual decision.

cards.front: What must you check before trusting an LLM judge in production?
cards.back: Its agreement with human labels, via a confusion matrix — not just a raw agreement percentage, which hides misses when errors are rare.
The point in error analysis where you stop finding new categories of failure — your signal to stop manually labeling traces.

cards.front: How many LLM-judge evaluators does a typical product actually need?
cards.back: 4–7 — not one for every conceivable failure mode.

cards.front: What is the “benevolent dictator” approach to evals?
cards.back: One domain expert is given authority to make the judgment calls on error analysis, instead of routing every decision through committee.
